svg.text: K4b BLADE ON THE ANVIL STICK — the mat brings the food, the blade cuts past the nose
Nothing is cut on a mat: the edge lands on a cheap POM stick; the cut food drops 65 mm onto the moving mat.
blade 300 mm, draw cut 8°, beam 90 × 12 cantilever 325 mm
column Ø 40 pull-down: 1 kN, 300 mm stroke, 250 mm/s
anvil stick POM 18 × 12 × 300 (ware, red / green), €10
finger comb 5–20 N · steam park after every raw cut
A SIDE SECTION at the nose: feed · hold · cut · drop · shingle

E feeds the slice thickness (1–40 mm), fingers hold, the edge lands on the stick
(landing found by motor current); the slice drops onto the mat that runs on by one step.
Carving a roast: 12 slices ≈ 1 min in carving order. For flat sheets the stick is lifted out.
B BLADE SEEN ALONG X: an inclined edge makes a draw cut

g.text: steam park: blade + fingers ≥ 95 °C for 60 s after a raw cut

svg.text: C CATCH POCKET: cutting while the arm works elsewhere
fork X 520: hem parked
E feeds; the mat sags into a pocket
over the dump funnel, ≈ 400 mm of mat:
two cucumbers of slices or half a
cabbage of shreds. The arm comes back
later, takes the hem and delivers.

g.text: 1/3 The capstan nose E pushes the food one slice-thickness past the blade plane, over the anvil stick
2/3 The sprung fingers press it down, then the inclined edge comes down and lands on the stick — never on a mat
3/3 The slice drops 65 mm onto the mat below, which runs on one step with the next feed: the slices lie shingled
